As well as inflating rents, the schemes served to transfer assets from Fred Trump to his children and nephew and lower the tax burden.[29]
Trump attracted public attention in 1978 with the launch of his family's first Manhattan venture: the renovation of the derelict Commodore Hotel, adjacent to Grand Central Terminal.[31] The financing was facilitated by a $400 million city property tax abatement arranged for him by his father who also, jointly with Hyatt, guaranteed a $70 million bank construction loan.[15][32] The hotel reopened in 1980 as the Grand Hyatt Hotel,[33] and that same year, he obtained rights to develop Trump Tower, a mixed-use skyscraper in Midtown Manhattan.[34] The building houses the headquarters of the Trump Corporation and Trump's PAC and was his primary residence until 2019.[35] In 1988, Trump acquired the Plaza Hotel with a loan from a consortium of 16 banks.[36] The hotel filed for bankruptcy protection in 1992, and a reorganization plan was approved a month later, with the banks taking control of the property.[37]
In 1995, he defaulted on over $3 billion of bank loans, and the lenders seized the Plaza Hotel along with most of his other properties in a "vast and humiliating restructuring" that allowed him to avoid personal bankruptcy.[38][39] The lead bank's attorney said of the banks' decision that they "all agreed that he'd be better alive than dead".[38] In 1996, Trump acquired and renovated the mostly vacant 71-story skyscraper at 40 Wall Street, later rebranded as the Trump Building.[40] In the early 1990s, he won the right to develop a 70-acre (28 ha) tract in the Lincoln Square neighborhood near the Hudson River
Struggling with debt from other ventures in 1994, he sold most of his interest in the project to Asian investors, who financed the project's completion, Riverside South.[41] Trump's last major construction project was the 92-story mixed-use Trump International Hotel and Tower in Chicago, which opened in 2008
In 2024, The New York Times and ProPublica reported that the Internal Revenue Service was investigating whether he had twice written off losses incurred through construction cost overruns and lagging sales of residential units in the building he had declared to be worthless on his 2008 tax return.[42]
In 1984, Trump opened Harrah's at Trump Plaza, a hotel and casino, with financing and management help from the Holiday Corporation.[43] It was unprofitable, and he paid Holiday $70 million in May 1986 to take sole control.[44] In 1985, he bought the unopened Atlantic City Hilton Hotel and renamed it Trump Castle.[45] Both casinos filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 1992.[46] Trump bought a third Atlantic City venue in 1988, the Trump Taj Mahal
It was financed with $675 million in junk bonds and completed for $1.1 billion, opening in April 1990.[43] He filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 1991
Under the provisions of the restructuring agreement, he gave up half his initial stake and personally guaranteed future performance.[47] To reduce his $900 million of personal debt, he sold the Trump Shuttle airline; his megayacht, the Trump Princess, which had been leased to his casinos and kept docked; and other businesses.[48] In 1995, Trump founded Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts (THCR), which assumed ownership of the Trump Plaza.[49] THCR purchased the Taj Mahal and the Trump Castle in 1996 and went bankrupt in 2004 and 2009, leaving him with 10 percent ownership.[43] He remained chairman until 2009.[50]
In 1985, Trump acquired the Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida.[51] In 1995, he converted the estate into a private club with an initiation fee and annual dues
He continued to use a wing of the house as a private residence.[52] He declared the club his primary residence in 2019.[35] He began building and buying golf courses in 1999, owning 17 golf courses by 2016.[53]
The Trump Organization often licensed the Trump name for consumer products and services, including foodstuffs, apparel, learning courses, and home furnishings.[54] Over 50 licensing or management deals involved Trump's name, generating at least $59 million for his companies.[55] By 2018, only two consumer goods companies continued to license his name.[54] During the 2000s, Trump licensed his name to residential property developments worldwide, 40 of which were never built.[56]
In 1970, Trump invested $70,000 to receive billing as coproducer of a Broadway comedy.[57] In September 1983, he purchased the New Jersey Generals, a team in the United States Football League
After the 1985 season, the league folded, largely due to his attempt to move to a fall schedule (when it would have competed with the National Football League [NFL] for audience) and trying to force a merger with the NFL by bringing an antitrust suit.[58] Trump and his Plaza Hotel hosted several boxing matches at the Atlantic City Convention Hall.[43][59] In 1989 and 1990, he lent his name to the Tour de Trump cycling stage race, an attempt to create an American equivalent of European races such as the Tour de France or the Giro d'Italia.[60] From 1986 to 1988, he purchased significant blocks of shares in various public companies while suggesting that he intended to take over the company and then sold his shares for a profit,[61] leading some observers to think he was engaged in greenmail.[62] The New York Times found that he initially made millions of dollars in such stock transactions, but "lost most, if not all, of those gains after investors stopped taking his takeover talk seriously".[61]
In 1988, Trump purchased the Eastern Air Lines Shuttle, financing the purchase with $380 million (equivalent to $1010 million in 2024)[19] in loans from a syndicate of 22 banks
He renamed the airline Trump Shuttle and operated it until 1992.[63] He defaulted on his loans in 1991, and ownership passed to the banks.[64] In 1996, he purchased the Miss Universe pageants, including Miss USA and Miss Teen USA.[65] Due to disagreements with CBS about scheduling, he took both pageants to NBC in 2002.[66][67] In 2007, he received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame for his work as producer of Miss Universe.[68] NBC and Univision dropped the pageants in June 2015 in reaction to his comments about Mexican immigrants.[69]
In 2005, Trump cofounded Trump University, a company that sold real estate seminars for up to $35,000
After New York State authorities notified the company that its use of "university" violated state law (as it was not an academic institution), its name was changed to the Trump Entrepreneur Initiative in 2010.[70] In 2013, the State of New York filed a $40 million civil suit against Trump University, alleging that the company made false statements and defrauded consumers
Additionally, two class actions were filed in federal court against Trump and his companies
Internal documents revealed that employees were instructed to use a hard-sell approach, and former employees testified that Trump University had defrauded or lied to its students.[71] Shortly after he won the 2016 presidential election, he agreed to pay a total of $25 million to settle the three cases.[72]
The Donald J
Trump Foundation was a private foundation established in 1988.[73] From 1987 to 2006, Trump gave his foundation $5.4 million, which had been spent by the end of 2006
After donating a total of $65,000 in 2007–2008, he stopped donating any personal funds to the charity,[74] which received millions from other donors, including $5 million from Vince McMahon.[75] The foundation gave to health- and sports-related charities, conservative groups,[76] and charities that held events at Trump properties.[74] In 2016, The Washington Post reported that the charity had committed several potential legal and ethical violations, including self-dealing and tax evasion.[77] Also in 2016, the New York attorney general stated the foundation had violated state law by soliciting donations without submitting to required annual external audits and ordered it to cease its fundraising activities in New York immediately.[78] Trump's team announced in December 2016 that the foundation would be dissolved.[79] In June 2018, the New York attorney general's office filed a civil suit against the foundation, Trump, and his adult children, seeking $2.8 million in restitution and additional penalties.[80] In December 2018, the foundation ceased operation and disbursed its assets to other charities.[81] In November 2019, a New York state judge ordered Trump to pay $2 million to a group of charities for misusing the foundation's funds, in part to finance his presidential campaign.[82]
According to a review of state and federal court files conducted by USA Today in 2018, Trump and his businesses had been involved in more than 4,000 state and federal legal actions.[83] While he has not filed for personal bankruptcy, his over-leveraged hotel and casino businesses in Atlantic City and New York filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection six times between 1991 and 2009.[28] They continued to operate while the banks restructured debt and reduced his shares in the properties.[28] During the 1980s, more than 70 banks had lent Trump $4 billion.[84] After his corporate bankruptcies of the early 1990s, most major banks, with the exception of Deutsche Bank, declined to lend to him.[85] After the January 6 Capitol attack, the bank decided not to do business with him or his affiliated company in the future.[86]
Trump has said he began his career with "a small loan of a million dollars" from his father and that he had to pay it back with interest.[87] He borrowed at least $60 million from his father, largely did not repay the loans, and received another $413 million (2018 equivalent, adjusted for inflation) from his father's company.[88][29] Posing as a Trump Organization official named "John Barron", Trump called journalist Jonathan Greenberg in 1984, trying to get a higher ranking on the Forbes 400 list of wealthy Americans.[89] Trump self-reported his net worth over a wide range: from minus $900 million in 1990[90] to $10 billion in 2015.[91] In 2015, Forbes estimated his net worth at $4.5 billion, based on interviews with more than 80 sources.[92] In 2025, the magazine estimated his net worth at $5.1 billion and ranked him the 700th wealthiest person in the world.[93]
Trump has published 19 books under his name, most written or cowritten by ghostwriters.[94] His first book, The Art of the Deal (1987), was a New York Times Best Seller, and was credited by The New Yorker with making Trump famous as an "emblem of the successful tycoon".[95] The book was ghostwritten by Tony Schwartz, who is credited as a coauthor
Trump had cameos in many films and television shows from 1985 to 2001.[96] Trump acquired his style of politics from professional wrestling—with its staged fights and name-calling.[97] He sporadically appeared for the professional wrestling company WWE from the late 1980s including Wrestlemania 23 in 2007.[98][99] Starting in the 1990s, Trump appeared 24 times as a guest on the nationally syndicated Howard Stern Show.[100] He had his own short-form talk radio program, Trumped!, from 2004 to 2008.[101] From 2011 until 2015, he was a guest commentator on Fox & Friends.[102] In 2021, Trump, who had been a member since 1989, resigned from SAG-AFTRA to avoid a disciplinary hearing regarding the January 6 attack.[103] Two days later, the union permanently barred him.[104]
Producer Mark Burnett made Trump a television star[105] when he created The Apprentice, which Trump hosted from 2004 to 2015 (including variant The Celebrity Apprentice)
On the shows, he was a superrich chief executive who eliminated contestants with the catchphrase "you're fired"
The New York Times called his portrayal "a highly flattering, highly fictionalized version" of himself.[106] The shows remade Trump's image for millions of viewers nationwide.[106][107] With the related licensing agreements, they earned him more than $400 million.[108]
Trump registered as a Republican in 1987; a member of the Independence Party, the New York state affiliate of the Reform Party, in 1999; a Democrat in 2001; a Republican in 2009; unaffiliated in 2011; and a Republican in 2012.[109]
In 1987, Trump placed full-page advertisements in major newspapers[110] expressing his views on foreign policy and how to eliminate the federal budget deficit.[111] In 1988, he approached Lee Atwater, asking to be put into consideration to be Republican nominee George H
W
Bush's running mate
Bush found the request "strange and unbelievable".[112][113] Trump was a candidate in the 2000 Reform Party presidential primaries for three months before he withdrew in February 2000.[114][115][116] In 2011, Trump considered challenging President Barack Obama in the 2012 election
He spoke at the Conservative Political Action Conference in February and gave speeches in states with early primaries.[117][118] In May 2011, he announced that he would not run.[117]
Trump announced his candidacy for the 2016 election in June 2015.[119][120] He campaigned as a rich, successful businessman and an outsider without political experience,[121][122][123] and claimed media bias against him.[124][125] His campaign statements were often opaque and suggestive,[126] and a record number were false.[127][128][129] He became the Republican front-runner in March 2016[130] and was declared the presumptive Republican nominee in May.[131]
Trump described NATO as "obsolete"[132][133] and espoused views described by The Washington Post as noninterventionist and protectionist.[134] His campaign platform emphasized renegotiating U.S.–China relations and free trade agreements such as NAFTA and strongly enforcing immigration laws
Other campaign positions included pursuing energy independence while opposing climate change regulations, modernizing services for veterans, repealing and replacing the Affordable Care Act, abolishing Common Core education standards, investing in infrastructure, simplifying the tax code while reducing taxes, and imposing tariffs on imports by companies that offshore jobs
He advocated increasing military spending and extreme vetting or banning of immigrants from Muslim-majority countries.[135] He promised to build a wall on the Mexico–U.S
border and vowed that Mexico would pay for it.[136] He pledged to deport millions of illegal immigrants residing in the U.S.,[137] and criticized birthright citizenship for incentivizing "anchor babies".[138] According to an analysis in Political Science Quarterly, Trump made "explicitly racist and sexist appeals to win over white voters" during his 2016 presidential campaign.[139] In particular, his campaign launch speech drew criticism for claiming Mexican immigrants were "bringing drugs, they're bringing crime, they're rapists";[140] in response, NBC fired him from Celebrity Apprentice.[141]
Trump's FEC-required reports listed assets above $1.4 billion and outstanding debts of at least $315 million.[142][143] He did not release his tax returns, contrary to the practice of every major candidate since 1976 and his promises in 2014 and 2015 to do so if he ran for office.[144][145] He said his tax returns were being audited, and that his lawyers had advised him against releasing them.[146] After a lengthy court battle to block release of his tax returns and other records to the Manhattan district attorney for a criminal investigation, including two appeals by Trump to the U.S
Supreme Court, in February 2021 the high court allowed the records to be released to the prosecutor for review by a grand jury.[147][148] In October 2016, portions of Trump's state filings for 1995 were leaked to a reporter from The New York Times
They show that he had declared a loss of $916 million that year, which could have let him avoid taxes for up to 18 years.[149]
Trump won 306 pledged electoral votes versus 232 for Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton
After elector defections on both sides, the official count was 304 to 227.[150] The fifth person to be elected president despite losing the popular vote,[c] he received nearly 2.9 million fewer votes than Clinton, 46.3% to her 48.25%.[151] He was the only president who neither served in the military nor held any government office prior to becoming president.[152] His election marked the return of a Republican undivided government.[d][153] Trump's victory sparked protests in major U.S
cities.[154][155]
Trump was inaugurated on January 20, 2017
The day after his inauguration, an estimated 2.6 million people worldwide, including 500,000 in Washington, D.C., protested against him in the Women's Marches.[156] During his first week in office, Trump signed six executive orders, including authorizing procedures for repealing the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act ("Obamacare"), withdrawal from the Trans-Pacific Partnership negotiations, advancement of the Keystone XL and Dakota Access Pipeline projects, and planning for a wall along the U.S
border with Mexico.[157]
Before being inaugurated, Trump moved his businesses into a revocable trust,[158][159] rather than a blind trust or equivalent arrangement "to cleanly sever himself from his business interests".[160] He continued to profit from his businesses and knew how his administration's policies affected them.[159][161] Although he said he would eschew "new foreign deals", the Trump Organization pursued operational expansions in Scotland, Dubai, and the Dominican Republic.[159][161] Lobbyists, foreign government officials, and Trump donors and allies generated hundreds of millions of dollars for his resorts and hotels.[162] Trump was sued for violating the Domestic and Foreign Emoluments Clauses of the U.S
Constitution, the first time that the clauses had been substantively litigated.[163] One case was dismissed in lower court.[164] Two were dismissed by the Supreme Court as moot after his term.[165]
During the campaign, Trump had pledged to donate his presidential salary[166] and profits from foreign patronage[167] to the U.S
government
He donated his salary to federal agencies and publicized each donation until July 2020
Federal agencies surveyed by The Washington Post in July 2021 reported not having received any gifts after that month.[168] Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington reported in 2024 that he had donated $448,000 of an estimated $13.6 million in payments from foreign governments in his first term.[169]
Trump took office at the height of the longest economic expansion in American history,[170] which began in 2009 and continued until February 2020, when the COVID-19 recession began.[171] In December 2017, he signed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017
It reduced tax rates for businesses and individuals and eliminated the penalty associated with the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate.[172][173] The Trump administration claimed that the act would not decrease government revenue, but 2018 revenues were 7.6 percent lower than projected.[174] Under Trump, the federal budget deficit increased by almost 50 percent, to nearly $1 trillion in 2019.[175] By the end of his term, the U.S
national debt increased by 39 percent, reaching $27.75 trillion, and the U.S
debt-to-GDP ratio hit a post-World War II high.[176] Trump also failed to deliver the $1 trillion infrastructure spending plan on which he had campaigned.[177]
Trump is the only modern U.S
president to leave office with a smaller workforce than when he took office, by three million people.[170][178] He rejects the scientific consensus on climate change.[179][180][181][182] He reduced the budget for renewable energy research by 40 percent and reversed Obama-era policies directed at curbing climate change.[183] He withdrew from the Paris Agreement, making the U.S
the only nation to not ratify it.[184] He aimed to boost the production and exports of fossil fuels.[185][186] Natural gas expanded under Trump, but coal continued to decline.[187][188] He rolled back more than 100 federal environmental regulations, including those that curbed greenhouse gas emissions, air and water pollution, and the use of toxic substances
He weakened protections for animals and environmental standards for federal infrastructure projects, and expanded permitted areas for drilling and resource extraction, such as allowing drilling in the Arctic Refuge.[189]
Trump dismantled federal regulations on health,[190][191] labor,[191] the environment,[192][191] and other areas, including a bill that made it easier for severely mentally ill persons to buy guns.[193] During his first six weeks in office, he delayed, suspended, or reversed ninety federal regulations,[194] often "after requests by the regulated industries".[195] The Institute for Policy Integrity found that 78 percent of his proposals were blocked by courts or did not prevail over litigation.[196] During his campaign, Trump vowed to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act.[197] In office, he scaled back the Act's implementation through executive orders.[198][199] He expressed a desire to "let Obamacare fail"; his administration halved the enrollment period and drastically reduced funding for enrollment promotion.[200][201] In June 2018, the Trump administration joined 18 Republican-led states in arguing before the Supreme Court that the elimination of the financial penalties associated with the individual mandate had rendered the Act unconstitutional.[202][203] Their pleading would have eliminated health insurance coverage for up to 23 million Americans, but was unsuccessful.[202] During the 2016 campaign, Trump promised to protect funding for Medicare and other social safety-net programs
In January 2020, he expressed willingness to consider cuts to them.[204]
In response to the opioid epidemic, Trump signed legislation in 2018 to increase funding for drug treatments, but was widely criticized for failing to make a concrete strategy.[205] He barred organizations that provide abortions or abortion referrals from receiving federal funds.[206] He said he supported "traditional marriage", but considered the nationwide legality of same-sex marriage "settled".[207] His administration rolled back key components of the Obama administration's workplace protections against discrimination of LGBTQ people.[208] His attempted rollback of anti-discrimination protections for transgender patients in August 2020 was halted by a federal judge after a Supreme Court ruling extended employees' civil rights protections to gender identity and sexual orientation.[209] Trump has said he is opposed to gun control, although his views have shifted over time.[210] His administration took an anti-marijuana position, revoking Obama-era policies that provided protections for states that legalized marijuana.[211] He is a long-time advocate of capital punishment,[212][213] and his administration oversaw the federal government execute 13 prisoners, more than in the previous 56 years combined, ending a 17-year moratorium.[214] In 2016, he said he supported the use of interrogation torture methods "a hell of a lot worse than waterboarding."[215][216]
Trump's comments on the 2017 Unite the Right rally, condemning "this egregious display of hatred, bigotry and violence on many sides" and stating that there were "very fine people on both sides", were criticized as implying a moral equivalence between the white supremacist demonstrators and the counter-protesters.[217] In a January 2018 discussion of immigration legislation, he reportedly referred to El Salvador, Haiti, Honduras, and African nations as "shithole countries".[218] His remarks were condemned as racist.[219]
In July 2019, Trump tweeted that four Democratic congresswomen—all minorities, three of whom are native-born Americans—should "go back" to the countries they "came from".[220] Two days later the House of Representatives voted 240–187, mostly along party lines, to condemn his "racist comments".[221] White nationalist publications and social media praised his remarks, which continued over the following days.[222] He continued to make similar remarks during his 2020 campaign.[223] In June 2020, during the George Floyd protests, federal law-enforcement officials used tear gas and other crowd control tactics to remove a largely peaceful crowd of lawful protesters from Lafayette Square, outside the White House.[224][225] Trump then posed with a Bible for a photo-op at the nearby St
John's Episcopal Church,[224][226][227] with religious leaders condemning both the treatment of protesters and the photo opportunity itself.[228] Many retired military leaders and defense officials condemned his proposal to use the U.S
military against anti-police-brutality protesters.[229]
During his first term, Trump granted 237 requests for clemency, fewer than all presidents since 1900 with the exception of George H
W
Bush and George W
Bush.[230] Only 25 of them had been vetted by the Justice Department's Office of the Pardon Attorney; the others were granted to people with personal or political connections to him, his family, and his allies, or recommended by celebrities.[231][232] In his last full day in office, he granted 73 pardons and commuted 70 sentences.[233] Several Trump allies were not eligible for pardons under Justice Department rules, and in other cases the department had opposed clemency.[231] The pardons of three military service members convicted of or charged with violent crimes were opposed by military leaders.[234]
As president, Trump described illegal immigration as an "invasion" of the United States[235] and drastically escalated immigration enforcement.[236][237] He implemented harsh policies against asylum seekers[237] and deployed nearly 6,000 troops to the U.S.–Mexico border to stop illegal crossings.[238] He reduced the number of refugees admitted to record lows, from an annual limit of 110,000 before he took office to 15,000 in 2021.[239][240][241] Trump also increased restrictions on granting permanent residency to immigrants needing public benefits.[242] One of his central campaign promises was to build a wall along the U.S.–Mexico border;[243] during his first term, the U.S
built 73 miles (117 km) of wall in areas without barriers and 365 miles (587 km) to replace older barriers.[244] In 2018, Trump's refusal to sign any spending bill unless it allocated funding for the border wall[245] resulted in the longest-ever federal government shutdown, for 35 days from December 2018 to January 2019.[246][247] The shutdown ended after he agreed to fund the government without any funds for the wall.[246] To avoid another shutdown, Congress passed a funding bill with $1.4 billion for border fencing in February.[248] Trump later declared a national emergency on the southern border to divert $6.1 billion of funding to the border wall[248] despite congressional disagreement.[249]
In January 2017, Trump signed an executive order that denied entry to citizens of six Muslim-majority countries for four months and from Syria indefinitely.[250][251] The order caused many protests and legal challenges that resulted in nationwide injunctions.[250][251][252] A revised order giving some exceptions was also blocked by courts,[253][254] but the Supreme Court ruled in June that the ban could be enforced on those lacking "a bona fide relationship with a person or entity" in the U.S.[255] Trump replaced the ban in September with a presidential proclamation extending travel bans to North Koreans, Chadians, and some Venezuelan officials, but excluded Iraq and Sudan.[256] The Supreme Court allowed that version to go into effect in December 2017,[257] and ultimately upheld the ban in 2019.[258] From 2017 to 2018, the Trump administration had a policy of family separation that separated over 4,400 children of illegal immigrants from their parents at the U.S.–Mexico border,[259][260] an unprecedented[261] policy sparked public outrage in the country.[262] Despite Trump initially blaming Democrats[263][264] and insisting he could not stop the policy with an executive order, he acceded to public pressure in June 2018 and mandated that illegal immigrant families be detained together unless "there is a concern" of risk for the child.[265][266] A judge later ordered that the families be reunited and further separations stopped except in limited circumstances,[267][268] though over 1,000 additional children were separated from their families after the order.[260]
Trump described himself as a "nationalist"[269] and his foreign policy as "America First".[270] He supported populist, neo-nationalist, and authoritarian governments.[271] Unpredictability, uncertainty, and inconsistency characterized foreign relations during his tenure.[270][272] Relations between the U.S
and its European allies were strained under Trump.[273] He criticized NATO allies and privately suggested that the U.S
should withdraw from NATO.[274][275] Trump supported many of the policies of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu.[276] In 2020, Trump hosted the signing of the Abraham Accords between Israel and the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain to normalize their foreign relations.[277]
Trump began a trade war with China in 2018 after imposing tariffs and other trade barriers he said would force China to end longstanding unfair trade practice and intellectual property infringement.[278] Trump weakened the toughest U.S
sanctions imposed after the 2014 Russian annexation of Crimea.[279][280] Trump praised and, according to some critics, rarely criticized Russian president Vladimir Putin,[281][282] though he opposed some actions of Russia's government.[283] He withdrew the U.S
from the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, citing alleged Russian noncompliance,[284] and supported Russia's possible return to the G7.[285] As North Korea's nuclear weapons were increasingly seen as a serious threat,[286] Trump became the first sitting U.S
president to meet a North Korean leader, meeting Kim Jong Un three times: in Singapore in June 2018, in Hanoi in February 2019, and in the Korean Demilitarized Zone in June 2019.[287] Talks in October 2019 broke down and no denuclearization agreement was reached.[288][289]
By the end of Trump's first year in office, 34 percent of his original staff had resigned, been fired, or been reassigned.[290] As of early July 2018[update], 61 percent of his senior aides had left[291] and 141 staffers had left in the previous year.[292] Both figures set a record for recent presidents.[293] Close personal aides to Trump quit or were forced out.[294] He publicly disparaged several of his former top officials.[295]
Trump had four White House chiefs of staff, marginalizing or pushing out several.[296] In May 2017, he dismissed FBI director James Comey, saying a few days later that he was concerned about Comey's role in the Trump–Russia investigations.[297][298] Three of Trump's 15 original cabinet members left or were forced to resign within his first year.[299][294] Trump was slow to appoint second-tier officials in the executive branch, saying many of the positions are unnecessary
In October 2017, there were hundreds of sub-cabinet positions without a nominee.[300] By January 8, 2019, of 706 key positions, 433 had been filled and he had no nominee for 264.[301]
Trump appointed 226 federal judges, including 54 to the courts of appeals and three to the Supreme Court: Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett.[302] His Supreme Court appointments politically shifted the Court to the right.[303][304][305] In the 2016 campaign, he pledged that Roe v
Wade would be overturned "automatically" if he were elected and given the opportunity to appoint two or three anti-abortion justices
He later took credit when Roe was overturned by Dobbs v
Jackson Women's Health Organization in 2022; all three of his Supreme Court nominees voted with the majority.[306][307] Trump disparaged courts and judges he disagreed with, often in personal terms, and questioned the judiciary's constitutional authority
His attacks on courts drew rebukes from observers, including sitting federal judges, concerned about the effect of his statements on the judicial independence and public confidence in the judiciary.[308][309]
Trump initially ignored public health warnings and calls for action from health officials within his administration.[310] Trump established the White House Coronavirus Task Force on January 29.[311] On March 27, he signed into law the CARES Act—a $2.2 trillion bipartisan economic stimulus bill—the largest stimulus in U.S
history.[312][313] After weeks of attacks to draw attention away from his slow response, Trump halted funding of the World Health Organization in April.[314] In April 2020, Republican-connected groups organized anti-lockdown protests against the measures state governments were taking to combat the pandemic;[315][316] Trump encouraged the protests on Twitter,[317] although the targeted states did not meet his administration's guidelines for reopening.[318] He repeatedly pressured federal health agencies to take actions he favored,[319] such as approving unproven treatments.[320][321] In October, Trump was hospitalized at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center for three days with a severe case of COVID-19.[322]
After he assumed office, Trump was the subject of increasing Justice Department and congressional scrutiny, with investigations covering his election campaign, transition, and inauguration, actions taken during his presidency, his private businesses, personal taxes, and charitable foundation.[323] There were ten federal criminal investigations, eight state and local investigations, and twelve congressional investigations.[324]
In July 2016, the FBI launched Crossfire Hurricane, an investigation into possible links between Russia and Trump's 2016 campaign.[325] After Trump fired Comey in May 2017, the FBI opened a second investigation into Trump's personal and business dealings with Russia.[326] In January 2017, three U.S
intelligence agencies jointly stated with "high confidence" that Russia interfered in the 2016 presidential election to favor Trump.[327][328] Many suspicious[329] links between Trump associates and Russian officials were discovered.[330][331][332] Trump told Russian officials he was unconcerned about Russia's election interference.[333] Crossfire Hurricane was later transferred to Robert Mueller's special counsel investigation;[334] the investigation into Trump's ties to Russia was ended by Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein after he told the FBI that Mueller would pursue the matter.[335][336] At the request of Rosenstein, the Mueller investigation examined criminal matters "in connection with Russia's 2016 election interference".[335] Mueller submitted his final report in March 2019.[337] The report found that Russia did interfere in 2016 to favor Trump[338] and that Trump and his campaign welcomed and encouraged the effort,[339][340][341] but that the evidence "did not establish" that Trump campaign members conspired or coordinated with Russia.[342][343] Trump claimed the report exonerated him despite Mueller writing that it did not.[344] The report also detailed potential obstruction of justice by Trump but "did not draw ultimate conclusions"[345][346] and left the decision to charge the laws to Congress.[347]
In April 2019, the House Oversight Committee issued subpoenas seeking financial details from Trump's banks, Deutsche Bank and Capital One, and his accounting firm, Mazars USA
He sued the banks, Mazars, and committee chair Elijah Cummings to prevent the disclosures.[348] In May, two judges ruled that both Mazars and the banks must comply with the subpoenas;[349][350][351] Trump's attorneys appealed.[352] In September 2022, Trump and the committee agreed to a settlement regarding Mazars, and the firm began turning over documents.[353]
Trump was impeached twice by the House of Representatives, though acquitted by the Senate on both occasions
The first impeachment arose from a whistleblower complaint that in 2019 Trump had pressured Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy to investigate Joe and Hunter Biden,[354] in an attempt to gain an advantage in the 2020 presidential election.[355] In December 2019, the House voted to impeach Trump for abuse of power and obstruction of Congress,[356] and the Senate acquitted him in February 2020.[357]
The second impeachment came after the January 6 Capitol attack, for which the House charged Trump with incitement of insurrection on January 13, 2021.[358] Trump left office on January 20, and was acquitted on February 13
Seven Republican senators voted for conviction.[359]
Trump filed to run for reelection only a few hours after becoming president in 2017.[360] He held his first reelection rally less than a month after taking office[361] and officially became the Republican nominee in August 2020.[362] Trump's campaign focused on crime, claiming that cities would descend into lawlessness if Democratic nominee Joe Biden won.[363] He repeatedly misrepresented Biden's positions[364][365] and appealed to racism.[366] Starting in early 2020, Trump sowed doubts about the election, claiming without evidence that it would be rigged and that widespread use of mail balloting would produce massive election fraud.[367][368] He blocked funding for the U.S
Postal Service, saying he wanted to prevent any increase in voting by mail.[369] He repeatedly refused to say whether he would accept the results if he lost and commit to a peaceful transition of power.[370][371]
Biden won the November 2020 election, receiving 81.3 million votes (51.3 percent) to Trump's 74.2 million (46.8 percent)[372][373] and 306 electoral votes to Trump's 232.[374] The Electoral College formalized Biden's victory on December 14.[374] Trump declared victory before the results were known on the morning after the election.[375] Days later, when Biden was projected the winner, Trump baselessly alleged election fraud.[376] As part of an effort to overturn the results, Trump and his allies filed many legal challenges to the results, which were rejected by at least 86 judges in both state and federal courts for having no factual or legal basis.[377][378]
Trump's allegations were also refuted by state election officials,[379] and the Supreme Court declined to hear a case asking it to overturn the results in four states won by Biden.[380] Trump repeatedly sought help to overturn the results, personally pressuring Republican local and state office-holders,[381] Republican legislators,[382] the Justice Department,[383] and Vice President Pence,[384] urging actions such as replacing presidential electors,[382] or that Georgia officials "find" votes and announce a "recalculated" result.[381] In the weeks after the election, Trump withdrew from public activities.[385] He initially blocked government officials from cooperating in Biden's presidential transition.[386][387] After three weeks, the administrator of the General Services Administration declared Biden the "apparent winner" of the election, allowing the disbursement of transition resources to his team.[388] While Trump said he recommended that the GSA begin transition protocols, he still did not formally concede.[389][390] Trump did not attend Biden's inauguration on January 20.[391]
In December 2020, reports emerged that U.S
military leaders were on high alert, and ranking officers had discussed what to do if Trump declared martial law.[392] CIA director Gina Haspel and Army general Mark Milley, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, grew concerned that Trump might attempt a coup or military action against China or Iran.[393][394] Milley insisted that he be consulted about any military orders from Trump, including the use of nuclear weapons.[395][396]
At noon on January 6, 2021, while Congress was certifying the presidential election results in the U.S
Capitol, Trump held a rally at the nearby Ellipse
Speaking from behind a glass barrier,[397] he called for the election to be overturned and urged his supporters to "fight like hell" and "take back our country" by marching to the Capitol.[398] His supporters then formed a mob that broke into the building, disrupting certification and causing the evacuation of Congress.[399] During the attack, Trump posted on social media but did not ask the rioters to disperse
In a tweet at 6 p.m., he told them to "go home with love & in peace", called them "great patriots", and restated that he had won the election.[400] Congress later reconvened and confirmed Biden's victory in the early hours of January 7.[401]
More than 140 police officers were injured, and five people died during or after the attack.[402][403] The event has been described as an attempted self-coup by Trump.[e]
Upon leaving the White House, Trump began living at Mar-a-Lago, establishing an office there as provided for by the Former Presidents Act.[407] His continuing false claims concerning the 2020 election were commonly referred to as the "big lie" by his critics, although in May 2021, he and many of his supporters began using the term to refer to the election itself.[408][409] The Republican Party used his false claims about the election to justify imposing new voting restrictions in its favor.[410][411][412] As of July 2022, he continued to pressure state legislators to overturn the election.[413] Unlike other former presidents, Trump continued to dominate his party; a 2022 profile in The New York Times described him as a modern party boss.[414] He continued fundraising, raising a war chest containing more than twice that of the Republican Party, and profited from fundraisers many Republican candidates held at Mar-a-Lago
Much of his focus was on party governance and installing in key posts officials loyal to him.[414] In the 2022 midterm elections, he endorsed over 200 candidates for various offices.[415] In February 2021, he registered a new company, Trump Media & Technology Group (TMTG), for providing "social networking services" to U.S
customers.[416][417] In March 2024, TMTG merged with special-purpose acquisition company Digital World Acquisition and became a public company.[418] In February 2022, TMTG launched Truth Social, a social media platform.[419]
In 2019, journalist E
Jean Carroll accused Trump of raping her in the 1990s and sued him for defamation over his denial.[420] Carroll sued him again in 2022 for battery and more defamation.[421] He was found liable for sexual abuse and defamation and ordered to pay $5 million in one case[422] and $83.3 million in the other.[422][423] In 2022, New York filed a civil lawsuit against Trump accusing him of inflating the Trump Organization's value to gain an advantage with lenders and banks.[424][425] He was found liable and ordered to pay $350 million plus interest.[425]
In connection with Trump's efforts to overturn the 2020 election and his involvement in the January 6 attack, in December 2022 the U.S
House committee on the attack recommended criminal charges against him for obstructing an official proceeding, conspiracy to defraud the United States, and inciting or assisting an insurrection.[426] In August 2023, a grand jury in Fulton County, Georgia, indicted him on 13 charges, including racketeering, for his efforts to subvert the 2020 election in the state.[427][428]
In January 2022, the National Archives and Records Administration retrieved 15 boxes of documents Trump had taken to Mar-a-Lago after leaving the White House, some of which were classified.[429] In the ensuing Justice Department investigation, officials retrieved more classified documents from his lawyers.[429] On August 8, 2022, FBI agents searched Mar-a-Lago for illegally held documents, including those in breach of the Espionage Act, collecting 11 sets of classified documents, some marked top secret.[430][431] A federal grand jury constituted by Special Counsel Jack Smith indicted Trump in June 2023 on 31 counts of "willfully retaining national defense information" under the Espionage Act, among other charges.[429][432][433] Trump pleaded not guilty.[434] In July 2024, judge Aileen Cannon dismissed the case, ruling Smith's appointment as special prosecutor was unconstitutional.[435]
In May 2024, Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records.[436] The case stemmed from evidence that he booked Michael Cohen's hush-money payments to adult film actress Stormy Daniels as business expenses to cover up his alleged 2006–2007 affair with Daniels during the 2016 election.[436][437] On January 10, 2025, the judge gave Trump a no-penalty sentence known as an unconditional discharge, saying that punitive requirements would have interfered with presidential immunity.[438] After his reelection, the 2020 election obstruction case and the classified documents case were dismissed without prejudice due to Justice Department policy against prosecuting sitting presidents.[439]
In November 2022, Trump announced his candidacy for the 2024 presidential election and created a fundraising account.[440][441] In March 2023, the campaign began diverting ten percent of the donations to his leadership PAC
His campaign had paid $100 million towards his legal bills by March 2024.[442][443]
During the campaign, Trump made increasingly violent and authoritarian statements.[444][445][446][447] He said that he would weaponize the FBI and the Justice Department against his political opponents[448][449] and use the military to target Democratic politicians and those that did not support his candidacy.[450][451] He used harsher and more dehumanizing anti-immigrant rhetoric than during his presidency.[452][453][454][455] His rhetoric, calling his political opponents "the enemy", vermin, and fascists, has been described by some historians and scholars as authoritarian, fascist,[f] and unlike anything a political candidate has ever said in American history.[460][451][461] Age and health concerns also arose during the campaign, with several medical experts highlighting an increase in rambling, tangential speech and behavioral disinhibition.[462]
Trump mentioned "rigged election" and "election interference" earlier and more frequently than in the 2016 and 2020 campaigns and refused to commit to accepting the 2024 election results.[463][464] Analysts for The New York Times described this as an intensification of his "heads I win; tails you cheated" rhetorical strategy; the newspaper stated that the claim of a rigged election had become the backbone of the campaign.[464]
On July 13, 2024, Trump was shot in the ear in an assassination attempt at a campaign rally in Butler Township, Pennsylvania.[465][466][467] Two days later, the 2024 Republican National Convention nominated him as their presidential candidate, with Senator JD Vance as his running mate.[468] In September, he was targeted but unharmed in an assassination attempt in Florida.[469] Trump won the election in November 2024 with 312 electoral votes to incumbent vice president Kamala Harris's 226.[470] He also won the popular vote with 49.8% to Harris's 48.3%.[471] His victory in 2024 was part of a global backlash against incumbent parties,[472][473] in part due to the 2021–2023 inflation surge.[474][475] Several outlets described his reelection as an extraordinary comeback.[476][477]
Trump began his second term upon his inauguration on January 20, 2025.[478] He became the oldest individual to assume the presidency,[479] the first president with a felony conviction, and the second person to serve two nonconsecutive terms as president.[480]
Upon taking office, Trump signed a series of executive orders
Many of these tested his legal authority, and drew immediate legal action.[481] He issued more executive orders on his first day than any other president.[482] Four days into his second term, analysis conducted by Time found that nearly two-thirds of his executive actions "mirror or partially mirror" proposals from Project 2025.[483] In his first weeks, several of his actions ignored or violated federal laws, regulations, and the Constitution according to American legal scholars.[484][485][486] In his administration's first month, Trump issued ninety executive orders, memorandums, and directives.[487] He used the government to target his political opponents and his actions against civil society were described by legal experts and hundreds of political scientists as authoritarian and contributing to democratic backsliding.[488][489] His orders and actions were challenged by over 300 lawsuits nationwide, with most of them still moving through the courts by July 2.[490][491]
Trump's second presidency was described as having fewer guardrails against conflicts of interest than his first,[492] and breaking with decades of ethical norms.[493] He maintained a publicly-traded company in Trump Media & Technology Group, and diversified it into financial services.[494] He pursued new overseas real estate deals involving state-affiliated entities, and had several branding and licensing deals selling Trump-branded merchandise.[492] He profited from events held at his hotels and golf courses and did not place his assets in a blind trust, as previous presidents had done.[495]
Trump repealed the previous administration's ethics guidelines and enforcement of laws prohibiting bribery[496][497] without establishing formal ethics guidelines for his political appointees, many of whom entered his administration with an "uncharacteristically large list of potential conflicts of interest".[498] He dropped corruption charges against politicians with ties to him[499] and paused enforcement of the law prohibiting companies operating in the U.S
to bribe foreign governments.[500]
Trump launched, promoted, and personally benefited from two cryptocurrency tokens ("meme coins"), $Trump and $Melania.[496][501] He also directly benefited from his family's cryptocurrency company World Liberty Financial, which engaged in an unprecedented mixing of private enterprise and government policy.[502]
In July 2025, the Trump administration accepted a $400 million luxury jet from Qatar to serve as Air Force One until the end of his second term and then be transferred to his presidential library
The retrofitting as Air Force One is estimated to cost up to $1 billion.[503]
Trump implemented a hiring freeze across the federal government and ordered telework of federal employees to be discontinued within 30 days.[504][505] He ordered a review of many career civil service positions with the intention of reclassifying them into at-will positions without job protections.[505][506][507] He initiated mass job terminations of federal employees,[508] which were described by legal experts as unprecedented or in violation of federal law,[509] with the intent of replacing them with workers more aligned with his agenda.[510] By late February, the administration had fired more than 30,000 people.[511] To facilitate further terminations, it adopted a novel legal interpretation that vastly expands the range of departments and agencies considered as having national security for their primary function,[512][513][514] declaring various federal workers' unions "hostile".[515][516] A late March executive order based on this interpretation excluded dozens of departments and agencies from federal labor-management relations programs, prompting them to sue to invalidate their collective bargaining agreements,[517][514] which could remove union protections from one million federal employees.[515][518] He ordered an end to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) projects in the federal government and placed employees in DEI offices on leave
He rescinded Executive Order 11246, which mandated affirmative action and nondiscrimination practices for federal contractors and was in place since 1965.[519][520]
Trump and Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency largely dismantled several federal agencies including USAID and the Department of Education, unilaterally fired several thousand staff, and reduced administrative functions to statutory minimums.[521][522][523] Some actions, such as attempts to dismantle the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, were paused by federal courts.[524] Many of his actions attempted to bring historically independent institutions under direct executive branch control in diminished forms.[525]
As in his first presidency, Trump frequently bypassed the Office of the Pardon Attorney.[526] He installed political loyalist Ed Martin who described the rationale for granting pardons as "No MAGA left behind".[527] Trump's pardons and grants of clemency favored political allies and loyalists,[528][529] and disproportionately pardoned "the powerful, famous, well-connected and wealthy" accused of white-collar crime.[529] Trump granted clemency to all January 6 rioters convicted or charged on his first day in office, including those who violently attacked police, by pardoning more than 1,500 and commuting the sentences of 14.[530][531]
Trump inherited a resilient economy from the Biden administration, with increasing economic growth, low unemployment, and declining inflation.[g]
Trump canceled and paused federal grants and made large cuts to scientific research.[538] He promoted climate change denial and misinformation,[539] and appointed oil, gas, and chemical lobbyists to the EPA to reverse climate regulations and pollution controls.[540] He declared a national energy emergency, allowing the suspension of environmental regulations, loosening the rules for fossil fuel extraction and limiting renewable energy projects.[541][542] He initiated a review of the "legality and continued applicability" of the EPA endangerment finding, which is the basis of most federal regulations on greenhouse gases,[543] and again withdrew the U.S
from the Paris Agreement on climate change.[544]
Dismantling government agencies enforcing the laws against political corruption and white-collar fraud,[545] Trump reduced the Department of Justice's Public Integrity Section from 30 to five lawyers,[546][547] dismissed 17 independent inspectors general at government agencies[548] and 12 members of independent oversight boards and watchdog agencies,[549] and disbanded the squad in the FBI's Washington field office that investigated allegations of fraud and corruption against government officials and members of Congress.[550][551] He pardoned or dropped charges against officials accused of corruption.[550]
Trump attributed societal problems to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives and wokeness.[552] Equating diversity with incompetence,[552] he reversed pro-diversity policies in the federal government.[553][554] His administration aggressively moved against the rights of transgender people and what it termed "gender ideology".[555][556] He sought to remake civil society to his preferences by executive order.[557] On DEI and antisemitism grounds, he threatened cultural institutions[558] and sixty universities,[559] and forced law firms to capitulate to his political agenda.[557]
In July 2025, Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act into law
The bill made the tax cuts of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act permanent and added additional tax deductions for a total of around $4.5 trillion, mostly benefiting the highest income brackets and costing people in the lowest income bracket $1,600 per year; increased funding for national defense, deportations, the border wall, and a missile shield; and removed tax credits for clean energy projects using renewable energy sources such as wind and solar power and for buyers of electric vehicles
The bill cut funding for Medicaid and SNAP and added additional work requirements for eligibility and a $35 co-payment for some Medicaid services; the cuts and additional requirements will take effect after the 2026 general election
The bill was projected by the Congressional Budget Office to increase the budget deficit by $3.4 trillion by 2034, cause 11.8 million people to lose Medicaid coverage, and eliminate SNAP benefits for three million people.[560][561]
In his first days in office, Trump instructed Border Patrol agents to summarily deport illegal immigrants crossing the border, disabling the CBP One app that was being used to schedule border crossings
He resumed the remain in Mexico policy, designated drug cartels as terrorist groups, and ordered construction to be resumed on a border wall.[562][563]
Deportation operations first focused on "target lists" of criminals formed prior to Trump's second term.[564] Then his administration removed asylum applicants who failed to meet requirements,[565] revoked the parole status of immigrants who entered the U.S
under CBP One and CHNV humanitarian parole,[563] attempted to remove birthright citizenship,[566] and suspended the Refugee Admissions Program.[567] In March, he used the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 to imprison illegal immigrants without trial—one by "administrative error"[568] and most without criminal records[h]—at the Terrorism Confinement Center in El Salvador.[570] He targeted activists, legal immigrants, tourists, and students with visas who expressed criticism of his policies or pro-Palestinian advocacy.[571]
Trump's second term foreign policy has been variously described as imperialist, expansionist,[572][573] isolationist, and autarkist, employing the "America First" ideology as its cornerstone.[574] His relations with allies were transactional and ranged from indifference to hostility, including threats of annexation.[575][576] He ordered the U.S
government to stop funding and working with the WHO and announced the U.S.'s intention to formally leave the WHO.[577][578][579]
In February 2025, Trump and Vice President Vance met with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the president of Ukraine, in the Oval Office
The meeting, which was televised live, was highly contentious as Trump and Vance berated Zelenskyy
Media outlets described it as an unprecedented public confrontation between an American president and a foreign head of state.[580][581]
Trump and his incoming administration helped broker a Gaza war ceasefire alongside the Biden administration, enacted a day prior to his inauguration.[582][583][584] In March, Israel broke the ceasefire.[584]
Trump's economic policies have been described as protectionist,[585] with Trump imposing tariffs on most countries, including large tariffs on major trading partners China, Canada, and Mexico.[586] He triggered a global trade war and brought tariffs to their highest level since the Smoot–Hawley Tariff Act during the Great Depression.[587][588] Economists argued that the administration misunderstood the relationship between trade deficits and tariffs, using flawed assumptions.[589] He suspended American financial contributions to the World Trade Organization.[590]
In his second term, Trump selected cabinet members with personal loyalty to him,[591][592] with the "focus on loyalty over subject-matter expertise".[592] In February 2025, the White House stated that Elon Musk was a special government employee.[593] Trump gave Musk's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) access to many federal government agencies.[593] Musk's teams operated in eighteen departments and agencies in the administration's first month,[594] including in the Treasury Department's $5 trillion payment system,[595] the Small Business Administration, the Office of Personnel Management, and the General Services Administration.[596] He nominated or appointed 23 former Fox News employees to his administration.[597]
Following legal setbacks, Trump increased his criticism of the judiciary and called for impeachment of federal judges who ruled against him.[598] He threatened, signed executive actions, and ordered investigations into his political opponents, critics, and organizations aligned with the Democratic Party.[599] By mid-July, a Washington Post analysis found he defied judges and the courts in roughly one third of all cases against him, actions which were described by legal experts as unprecedented for any presidential administration.[600] His defiance of court orders and a claimed right to disobey the courts raised fears among legal experts of a constitutional crisis.[601] Multiple analyses conducted by academic scholars and the New York Times found that both Republican and Democratic judicial appointees have found numerous constitutional and statutory flaws with Trump administration policies.[602] He engaged in an unprecedented targeting of law firms and lawyers that previously represented positions adverse to himself.[603][604]
Beginning with his 2016 campaign, Trump's politics and rhetoric led to the creation of a political movement known as Trumpism.[605] His political positions are populist,[606][607] more specifically described as right-wing populist.[608][609] He has been described as embracing far-right extremism,[610][611] and he helped bring far-right fringe ideas and organizations into the mainstream.[612] Many of his actions and rhetoric have been described as authoritarian and contributing to democratic backsliding.[613][614] Trump pushed for an expansion of presidential power under a maximalist interpretation of the unitary executive theory.[615][616] His political base has been compared to a cult of personality.[i]
Trump's rhetoric and actions have been accused of creating and exacerbating anger and distrust through the use of an "us" versus "them" narrative.[624] He explicitly and routinely disparages racial, religious, and ethnic minorities,[625] and scholars consistently find that racial animus regarding blacks, immigrants, and Muslims are the best predictors of support for Trump.[626] His rhetoric has been described as using fearmongering and demagogy which intensified during his 2024 presidential campaign.[627] He has said that he believes real power comes from fear.[628] The alt-right movement coalesced around and supported his candidacy, due in part to its opposition to multiculturalism and immigration.[629][630][631] He has a strong appeal to evangelical Christian voters and Christian nationalists,[632] and his rallies take on the symbols, rhetoric, and agenda of Christian nationalism.[633] Trump has also used anti-communist sentiment in his rhetoric, regularly calling his opponents "communists" and "Marxists".[634][635]
Many of Trump's comments and actions have been characterized as racist.[636] In a 2018 national poll, about half of respondents said he is racist; a greater proportion believed that he emboldened racists.[637] Several studies and surveys found that racist attitudes fueled his political ascent and were more important than economic factors in determining the allegiance of Trump voters.[638] Racist and Islamophobic attitudes are strong indicators of support for Trump.[639] He has been accused of racism for insisting a group of five black and Latino teenagers were guilty of raping a white woman in the 1989 Central Park jogger case, even after they were exonerated in 2002.[640]
In 2011, Trump became the leading proponent of the racist "birther" conspiracy theory that Barack Obama, the first black U.S
president, was not born in the United States.[641] He claimed credit for pressuring the government to publish Obama's birth certificate, which he considered fraudulent.[642] He acknowledged that Obama was born in the U.S
in September 2016,[643] though reportedly expressed birther views privately in 2017.[644] During the 2024 presidential campaign, he made false attacks against the racial identity of his opponent, Kamala Harris, that were described as reminiscent of the birther conspiracy theory.[645] His 2024 campaign made extensive use of dehumanizing language and racial stereotypes.[646][647][648][649] In 2025, he promoted false claims of white genocide in South Africa[650] and created the White South African refugee program.[651]
Trump has a history of belittling women when speaking to the media and on social media.[652][653] He made lewd comments, disparaged women's physical appearances, and referred to them using derogatory epithets.[653] At least 25 women publicly accused him of sexual misconduct, including rape, kissing without consent, groping, looking under women's skirts, and walking in on naked teenage pageant contestants
He has denied the allegations.[654] In October 2016, a 2005 "hot mic" recording surfaced in which he bragged about kissing and groping women without their consent, saying that, "when you're a star, they let you do it
You can do anything
..
Grab 'em by the pussy."[655] He characterized the comments as "locker-room talk".[656][657] The incident's widespread media exposure led to his first public apology, videotaped during his 2016 presidential campaign.[658]
Trump has been identified as a key figure in increasing political violence in the U.S., both for and against him.[659][660][661] He is described as embracing extremism, conspiracy theories such as Q-Anon, and far-right militia movements to a greater extent than any modern American president,[610][662] and engaging in stochastic terrorism.[663][664]
Research suggests Trump's rhetoric is associated with an increased incidence of hate crimes,[665][666] and that he has an emboldening effect on expressing prejudicial attitudes due to his normalization of explicit racial rhetoric.[667] During his 2016 campaign, he urged or praised physical attacks against protesters or reporters.[668][669] Numerous defendants investigated or prosecuted for violent acts and hate crimes cited his rhetoric in arguing that they were not culpable or should receive leniency.[670][671] A nationwide review by ABC News in May 2020 identified at least 54 criminal cases, from August 2015 to April 2020, in which he was invoked in direct connection with violence or threats of violence mostly by white men and primarily against minorities.[672] Trump's refusal to condemn the white supremacist Proud Boys during a 2020 presidential debate[673] and his comment, "Proud Boys, stand back and stand by", were said to have led to increased recruitment for the pro-Trump group.[674] Counterterrorism researchers described his normalization and revisionist history of the January 6 Capitol attack, and grant of clemency to all January 6 rioters, as encouraging future political violence.[675][676]
Since before his first presidency, Trump has promoted numerous conspiracy theories, including Obama "birtherism", global warming being a hoax, and alleged Ukrainian interference in U.S
elections.[677][678][679] After the 2020 presidential election, he promoted conspiracy theories for his defeat that were characterized as "the big lie".[680][681]
Trump frequently makes false statements in public remarks[685][127] to an extent unprecedented in American politics.[685][686][687] His falsehoods are a distinctive part of his political identity[686] and have been described as firehosing.[688] His false and misleading statements were documented by fact-checkers, including at The Washington Post, which tallied 30,573 false or misleading statements made by him during his first presidency,[682] increasing in frequency over time.[689]
Some of Trump's falsehoods were inconsequential,[690][691] while others had more far-reaching effects, such as his unproven promotion of antimalarial drugs as a treatment for COVID-19,[692][693] causing a U.S
shortage of these drugs and panic-buying in Africa and South Asia.[694][695] Other misinformation, such as misattributing a rise in crime in England and Wales to the "spread of radical Islamic terror", served his domestic political purposes.[696] His attacks on mail-in ballots and other election practices weakened public faith in the integrity of the 2020 presidential election,[697][698] while his disinformation about the pandemic delayed and weakened the national response to it.[699][700][701] He habitually does not apologize for his falsehoods.[702] Until 2018, the media rarely referred to his falsehoods as lies, including when he repeated demonstrably false statements.[703][704][705]
Trump's social media presence attracted worldwide attention after he joined Twitter in 2009
He posted frequently during his 2016 campaign and as president until Twitter banned him after the January 6 attack.[706] He often used Twitter to communicate directly with the public and sideline the press;[707] in 2017, his press secretary said that his tweets constituted official presidential statements.[708]
After years of criticism for allowing Trump to post misinformation and falsehoods, Twitter began to tag some of his tweets with fact-checks in May 2020.[709] In response, he said social media platforms "totally silence" conservatives and he would "strongly regulate, or close them down".[710] After the January 6 attack, he was banned from Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, and other platforms.[711] The loss of his social media presence diminished his ability to shape events[712][713] and correlated with a dramatic decrease in the volume of misinformation on Twitter.[714] In February 2022, he launched social media platform Truth Social where he attracted a fraction of his Twitter following.[715] Elon Musk, after acquiring Twitter, reinstated his Twitter account in November 2022.[716][717] Meta Platforms' two-year ban lapsed in January 2023, allowing him to return to Facebook and Instagram.[718]
Trump sought media attention throughout his career, maintaining a "love-hate" relationship with the press.[719] In the 2016 campaign, he benefited from a record amount of free media coverage,[720] estimated at $2 billion.[721] As a candidate and as president, he frequently accused the press of bias, calling it the "fake news media" and "the enemy of the people".[722]
The first Trump presidency reduced formal press briefings from about one hundred in 2017 to about half that in 2018 and to two in 2019; they also revoked the press passes of two White House reporters, which were restored by the courts.[723] Trump's 2020 presidential campaign sued The New York Times, The Washington Post, and CNN for defamation in opinion pieces about his stance on Russian election interference
All the suits were dismissed.[724][725] By 2024, Trump repeatedly voiced support for outlawing political dissent and criticism,[726] and said that reporters should be prosecuted for not divulging confidential sources and media companies should possibly lose their broadcast licenses for unfavorable coverage of him.[727]
Following his reelection, Trump launched lawsuits and created blacklists against certain media outlets, and took over the process run by the White House Correspondents' Association to choose what outlets have access to him.[728] Rather than comply with a court order to restore Associated Press access, the White House made a policy of limited access for all wire services.[729] The Federal Communications Commission launched investigations into media outlets accused of bias against him.[730]
In 1977, Trump married Czech model Ivana Zelníčková.[731] They had three children: Donald Jr
(b
1977), Ivanka (b
1981), and Eric (b
1984)
The couple divorced in 1990, following his affair with model and actress Marla Maples.[732] He and Maples married in 1993 and divorced in 1999
They have one daughter, Tiffany (b
1993), whom Maples raised in California.[733] In 2005, he married Slovenian model Melania Knauss.[734] They have one son, Barron (b
2006).[735]
Trump says he has never drunk alcohol, smoked cigarettes, or used drugs.[736][737] He sleeps about four or five hours a night.[738][739] He has called golfing his "primary form of exercise", but usually does not walk the course.[740] He considers exercise a waste of energy because he believes the body is "like a battery, with a finite amount of energy", which is depleted by exercise.[741][742] In 2015, his campaign released a letter from his longtime personal physician, Harold Bornstein, stating that he would "be the healthiest individual ever elected to the presidency".[743] In 2018, Bornstein said Trump had dictated the contents of the letter and that three of Trump's agents had seized his medical records in a February 2017 raid on Bornstein's office.[743][744]
Trump said in 2016 that he was a Presbyterian and a Protestant.[745][746] In 2020, he said he was a nondenominational Christian.[747] However, many have questioned the depth of these religious affiliations
A survey during Trump's first presidency (2017–2021) showed that 63 percent of Americans did not believe he was religious, despite his professed Christian affiliation, and that only 44 percent of Americans believed that Trump was a Christian.[748] Some of Trump's comments on the Bible or Christian practice have led critical observers to suggest that his knowledge of Christianity is superficial or erroneous, and few biographers have described Trump as deeply or even particularly religious.[749][750]
In Trump's first term, from 2017 to 2020, international approval ratings of U.S
leadership dropped from about 22 percent in a Gallup poll[751] of 134 countries to just 16 percent—lower than China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin—in a Pew Research poll[752] of 13 countries
In 2017, estimation of U.S
leadership declined most among allies.[753]
Domestically, in his first term, Trump had chiefly partisan support: 88 percent among Republicans and 7 percent among Democrats.[754] In a 2021 Gallup poll, he was the only president never to reach a 50 percent approval rating, and he was the first not to be named most admired in his first year in office.[755]
In his second term's first quarter according to Gallup, Trump's approval rating was 45 percent—somewhat better than his first term, and far below the 60 percent average of other presidents
Support remained polarized; he had the approval of 90 percent among Republicans, 37 percent among independents, and 4 percent among Democrats.[756]
In C-SPAN's 2021 survey of presidential historians,[757] historians ranked Trump as the fourth-worst president
He rated lowest in the leadership characteristics categories for moral authority and administrative skills.[758][759] The Siena College Research Institute's 2022 survey ranked him third-worst
He was ranked near the bottom in all categories except for luck, willingness to take risks, and party leadership, and ranked last in several categories.[760] In 2018 and 2024, members of the American Political Science Association ranked him the worst president.[761][762]
A large language model (LLM) is a language model trained with self-supervised machine learning on a vast amount of text, designed for natural language processing tasks, especially language generation.
The largest and most capable LLMs are generative pretrained transformers (GPTs), which are largely used in generative chatbots such as ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude
LLMs can be fine-tuned for specific tasks or guided by prompt engineering.[1] These models acquire predictive power regarding syntax, semantics, and ontologies[2] inherent in human language corpora, but they also inherit inaccuracies and biases present in the data they are trained in.[3]
Before the emergence of transformer-based models in 2017, some language models were considered large relative to the computational and data constraints of their time
In the early 1990s, IBM's statistical models pioneered word alignment techniques for machine translation, laying the groundwork for corpus-based language modeling
A smoothed n-gram model in 2001, such as those employing Kneser-Ney smoothing, trained on 300 million words achieved state-of-the-art perplexity on benchmark tests at the time.[4] During the 2000s, with the rise of widespread internet access, researchers began compiling massive text datasets from the web ("web as corpus"[5]) to train statistical language models.[6][7]
Moving beyond n-gram models, researchers started in 2000 to use neural networks to learn language models.[8] Following the breakthrough of deep neural networks in image classification around 2012,[9] similar architectures were adapted for language tasks
This shift was marked by the development of word embeddings (eg, Word2Vec by Mikolov in 2013) and sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models using LSTM
In 2016, Google transitioned its translation service to neural machine translation (NMT), replacing statistical phrase-based models with deep recurrent neural networks
These early NMT systems used LSTM-based encoder-decoder architectures, as they preceded the invention of transformers.
At the 2017 NeurIPS conference, Google researchers introduced the transformer architecture in their landmark paper "Attention Is All You Need"
This paper's goal was to improve upon 2014 seq2seq technology,[10] and was based mainly on the attention mechanism developed by Bahdanau et al
in 2014.[11] The following year in 2018, BERT was introduced and quickly became "ubiquitous".[12] Though the original transformer has both encoder and decoder blocks, BERT is an encoder-only model
Academic and research usage of BERT began to decline in 2023, following rapid improvements in the abilities of decoder-only models (such as GPT) to solve tasks via prompting.[13]
Although decoder-only GPT-1 was introduced in 2018, it was GPT-2 in 2019 that caught widespread attention because OpenAI claimed to have initially deemed it too powerful to release publicly, out of fear of malicious use.[14] GPT-3 in 2020 went a step further and as of 2025[update] is available only via API with no offering of downloading the model to execute locally
But it was the 2022 consumer-facing chatbot ChatGPT that received extensive media coverage and public attention.[15] The 2023 GPT-4 was praised for its increased accuracy and as a "holy grail" for its multimodal capabilities.[16] OpenAI did not reveal the high-level architecture and the number of parameters of GPT-4
The release of ChatGPT led to an uptick in LLM usage across several research subfields of computer science, including robotics, software engineering, and societal impact work.[13] In 2024 OpenAI released the reasoning model OpenAI o1, which generates long chains of thought before returning a final answer.[17] Many LLMs with parameter counts comparable to those of OpenAI's GPT series have been developed.[18]
Since 2022, source-available models have been gaining popularity, especially at first with BLOOM and LLaMA, though both have restrictions on the field of use
Mistral AI's models Mistral 7B and Mixtral 8x7b have the more permissive Apache License
In January 2025, DeepSeek released DeepSeek R1, a 671-billion-parameter open-weight model that performs comparably to OpenAI o1 but at a much lower cost.[19]
Since 2023, many LLMs have been trained to be multimodal, having the ability to also process or generate other types of data, such as images or audio
These LLMs are also called large multimodal models (LMMs).[20]
As of 2024, the largest and most capable models are all based on the transformer architecture
Some recent implementations are based on other architectures, such as recurrent neural network variants and Mamba (a state space model).[21][22][23]
As machine learning algorithms process numbers rather than text, the text must be converted to numbers
In the first step, a vocabulary is decided upon, then integer indices are arbitrarily but uniquely assigned to each vocabulary entry, and finally, an embedding is associated to the integer index
Algorithms include byte-pair encoding (BPE) and WordPiece
There are also special tokens serving as control characters, such as [MASK] for masked-out token (as used in BERT), and [UNK] ("unknown") for characters not appearing in the vocabulary
Also, some special symbols are used to denote special text formatting
